question: Work, Energy and Power: Define work and write its SI unit.
gold_answer:
# Introduction

---

## Definition

Work is defined as the measure of energy transfer that occurs when an external force acts on an object and causes it to move through a displacement distance. 

Work is a scalar quantity calculated as the dot product of the applied force vector and the displacement vector.

---

## Characteristics

* **Directional Orientation Dependency:** Work value can scale as positive, negative, or zero depending on the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
* **Zero Work Scenarios:** No work is performed if the object remains stationary ($\Delta x = 0$) or if the applied force vector acts at a right angle ($90^\circ$) relative to the motion.

---

## Formula

The mathematical dot product defining mechanical work:

$$W = Fs \cos(\theta)$$

Where:
* $W$ represents the work scalar value
* $F$ represents the magnitude of the applied force vector
* $s$ represents the magnitude of the displacement vector
* $\theta$ represents the angle between the force and displacement paths

---

## Metric System Units

The standard SI unit of work is the **Joule ($\text{J}$)**, which is defined as the work performed when a constant force of $1 \text{ Newton}$ displaces an object through a distance of $1 \text{ meter}$ along its line of action.

$$1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N} \cdot \text{m} = 1 \text{ kg} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$$

---

## Summary

Work measures mechanical energy conversion, directly proportional to force intensity and displacement length, with a dependency on their mutual vector alignment angle.
candidate_response:
# Work, Energy and Power

---

## What is Work?

In physics, **work** is said to be done when a **force applied on an object causes displacement** in the direction of the force.

---

## Definition

> Work is defined as the product of the force applied on an object and the displacement produced in the direction of the force.

---

## Formula

$$W = F \cdot d \cdot \cos\theta$$

**Where:**

| Symbol | Meaning | SI Unit |
|--------|---------|---------|
| $W$ | Work done | Joule (J) |
| $F$ | Applied Force | Newton (N) |
| $d$ | Displacement | Metre (m) |
| $\theta$ | Angle between Force and Displacement | Degrees / Radians |

---

## SI Unit of Work

$$1 \text{ Joule} = 1 \text{ Newton} \times 1 \text{ Metre}$$

$$1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N·m}$$

> **The SI unit of Work is the Joule (J)**, named after the physicist **James Prescott Joule**.

**1 Joule** is defined as the work done when a force of **1 Newton** displaces an object by **1 metre** in the direction of the force.

---

## Special Cases

| Condition | Angle $\theta$ | Work Done |
|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| Force and displacement in **same direction** | $0°$ | $W = Fd$ (Maximum) |
| Force applied at an **angle** | $0° < \theta < 90°$ | $W = Fd\cos\theta$ |
| Force **perpendicular** to displacement | $90°$ | $W = 0$ |
| Force **opposite** to displacement | $180°$ | $W = -Fd$ (Negative Work) |

---

## Key Conditions for Work to be Done

Work is done **only if** all three conditions are met:

- ✅ A **force** must be applied
- ✅ The object must undergo **displacement**
- ✅ There must be a **component of force** in the direction of displacement

---

## Quick Example

A person pushes a box with a force of **10 N** and it moves **3 metres** in the same direction.

$$W = F \times d = 10 \times 3 = 30 \text{ J}$$

> **Work done = 30 Joules**
